tagline: Earth-lodge traces and a reconstructed fort beside the Missouri
intro: River bluffs, broad plains and bottomland forests meet at the Knife and Missouri rivers near Stanton. At the Washburn end of the journey, the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center overlooks the Missouri and adjoins a rest stop serving Highways 83 and 200A.

Travel here entered an established agricultural and trading landscape: Hidatsa and Mandan people traded corn alongside furs and other goods. The Lewis and Clark Expedition built Fort Mandan for the winter of 1804–1805. When the party returned in August 1806, the fort had burned; later, the Missouri eroded its former site.

Start with the Knife River villages north of Stanton, then continue toward the Fort Clark site west of Washburn. Near Washburn, Hensler lies beside railroad tracks close to Highway 200 Alternate. Finish at the interpretive center and the separate Fort Mandan reconstruction, about two miles apart.

moments.title: Knife River Indian Villages
moments.text: Circular depressions mark earth lodges at the Knife River villages, where collapsed walls and roofs left visible rims. Some dwellings measured as much as 40 feet across. The villages formed a trading and agricultural center; women managed extensive gardens of corn, beans, squash and sunflowers. Sakakawea, a Shoshone captive, lived in one of the Knife River villages. The historic site preserves village remains, cache pits and traces of travois trails. Wooden lodge structures were covered with willows, dried grass and earth. A central fireplace vented through a hole in the roof.

moments.title: Fort Clark
moments.text: Lodge depressions and an unmarked cemetery with more than 800 graves remain at Fort Clark. Mandan people built an earth-lodge settlement on the Missouri bluffs in 1822. James Kipp of the American Fur Company established a trading post south of the village in 1830. In 1837, passengers infected with smallpox arrived aboard the St. Peters; the ensuing epidemic killed approximately ninety percent of the villagers. Arikara people moved into the abandoned village in 1838. A second trading post followed in 1850. Further epidemics struck before an attack by the Dakota in 1861 led to permanent abandonment of the fort.

moments.title: Washburn
moments.text: The Fort Mandan near Washburn is a reconstruction of the expedition’s winter quarters. The original was triangular, built from cottonwood cut along the riverbanks, with its gate facing the Missouri. Its precise location is uncertain and is believed to lie beneath the river. The reconstruction follows materials and designs described in the expedition journals. Nearby, the interpretive center also addresses Mandan and Hidatsa farming cultures and the fur trade at Fort Clark. Reproduction furnishings include bunks, map-making tools and a blacksmith’s forge. Walking trails follow the property and the river beside it.
